title: Topological Sort: Order Tasks by Dependency
oneLiner: Given a pile of tasks with prerequisites, find a valid order to do them in -- or discover there isn't one, because some of them depend on each other in a loop.
keyTakeaway: Kahn's algorithm processes tasks by IN-DEGREE (how many unfinished prerequisites each task still has): repeatedly take any task with zero remaining prerequisites, "do" it, and decrement its dependents' counts. If every task eventually reaches zero, that processing order IS a valid topological order; if some tasks never reach zero, they're stuck in a CYCLE and no valid order exists.
explanation:
Given n tasks and a list of prerequisite pairs (a, b) meaning "a must be done before b," find a valid order to do every task in -- or determine no valid order exists. This is a DIRECTED graph problem: each prerequisite pair is an edge from a to b, and the question is whether that directed graph has a cycle (impossible) or is a DAG (directed acyclic graph -- always orderable).

Kahn's algorithm solves it by tracking each task's IN-DEGREE: how many prerequisites it still has outstanding. Start by finding every task with in-degree 0 (no prerequisites at all) -- those can go first. Process one: add it to the order, then decrement the in-degree of every task that depended on it (one of its prerequisites is now satisfied). Any task that just hit in-degree 0 becomes available too. Repeat until every task is processed. When multiple tasks are available at the same time, this lesson always processes the SMALLEST-numbered one, so there's exactly one correct order to check against.

If the process ever runs out of in-degree-0 tasks while tasks remain unprocessed, those remaining tasks form a CYCLE -- each is waiting on a prerequisite that's itself waiting, all the way around, so none of them can ever legally go first. That's the graph-native reason "can I finish all these courses" and "is a valid order possible" are the same question.

Watch the in-degree array below drop to zero for each task as its prerequisites get satisfied one by one.

recognitionSignals: The problem describes tasks/courses/steps with PREREQUISITES or DEPENDENCIES, and asks for a valid order to do them in (or whether a valid order even exists).
The dependency structure is a DIRECTED graph, and "cycle = impossible" is part of the problem (you can't finish a course that indirectly depends on itself).
gotchas: A cycle means SOME tasks never reach in-degree 0 -- if the algorithm finishes with fewer tasks ordered than exist in total, that's the cycle signal, not a bug in the algorithm.

This builds a directed graph -- prerequisite (a, b) means an edge FROM a TO b (a unlocks b), the opposite direction from how some problem statements phrase "b depends on a." Double check which direction a problem's pairs mean.
confusableWith: Graphs: BFS Traversal (Fundamentals track) also processes nodes via a queue-like frontier, but on an UNDIRECTED graph with no notion of prerequisites -- topological sort's in-degree tracking and directed edges are what make ORDERING (not just reachability) meaningful.

complexity.note: Building the in-degrees and adjacency lists is one pass over the E edges. This lesson always takes the smallest-numbered ready task, so the ready pool is a min-priority queue: each of the V tasks is pushed and popped once at O(log V), and each edge is decremented once, giving O(V log V + E). (Kahn's algorithm with a plain FIFO queue, when any valid order will do, is O(V + E).) Space is the adjacency lists, O(V + E), plus the in-degree array, the queue and the order, O(V) each.

referenceSolutions.python:
import heapq

def topological_order(n, prerequisites):
    in_degree = [0] * n
    nxt = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for before, after in prerequisites:
        nxt[before].append(after)
        in_degree[after] += 1

    # A min-heap, so ties always go to the smallest-numbered task.
    ready = [i for i in range(n) if in_degree[i] == 0]
    heapq.heapify(ready)

    order = []
    while ready:
        task = heapq.heappop(ready)
        order.append(task)
        for after in nxt[task]:
            in_degree[after] -= 1
            if in_degree[after] == 0:
                heapq.heappush(ready, after)
    return order if len(order) == n else []  # leftovers mean a cycle
